title: The Etruscans Next Door
objective: After this level you can describe who the Etruscans were and what Rome borrowed from them.
summary: The Etruscans of Tuscany were early Italy’s great power. Rome had Etruscan kings and borrowed the fasces and haruspicy from them.

cards.headline: Before Rome was a great power, it lived next to one.
cards.body: The Etruscans were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Rome borrowed a lot from them, even, tradition says, some of its kings.

cards.headline: Rome’s powerful neighbors
cards.body: North of Rome, in Etruria, mostly what is now Tuscany, lived the Etruscans. They weren’t one kingdom but a set of independent cities, and they were among the most powerful peoples of early Italy. Their language was unrelated to Latin, and it is still only partly understood. Rome’s big neighbors next door, and we still can’t fully read their mail.

cards.headline: Etruscan kings
cards.body: Here’s the twist. According to Roman tradition, the last three kings of Rome were Etruscans. Historians can’t vouch for every detail, but the bigger picture holds: young Rome grew up under strong Etruscan influence. For a while, the neighbors weren’t just next door. They were on the throne.

cards.headline: What Rome borrowed
cards.body: Some of Rome’s most Roman-looking things were imports. Take the fasces, a bundle of rods around an axe. Attendants carried it in front of officials as a sign of their authority, and it came from the Etruscans. So did haruspicy: reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals. A way to show power and a way to read the gods, both borrowed from next door.
cards.callout: Fasces: rods and an axe, the symbol of authority

questions.prompt: Match each Etruscan name with what it was.

pairs.right: A bundle of rods around an axe

questions.explanation: Etruria was mostly what is now Tuscany. The fasces was a bundle of rods around an axe, and haruspicy meant reading omens in the organs of sacrificed animals.

questions.prompt: Attendants carried the fasces in front of a Roman official to signal _____.

options.label: a declaration of war
options.rationale: They were carried in peacetime too.

questions.explanation: The fasces, rods around an axe, were a visible sign of an official’s power.

questions.prompt: Why would both Etruscans and Latins care about the site of Rome?

options.label: It controlled a Tiber crossing on a trade route
It was the only safe harbor on Italy’s west coast
It was sacred to Etruscan gods
options.rationale: The draw was trade and crossing.

questions.explanation: A river crossing on the route between coast and inland Italy made the site valuable to anyone who traded.
